case.case_title: Vinayagamoorthy Attorney-at-Law (on behalf of Wimalenthiran) v. The Army Commander and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 26/94, decided on 25 November 1996

clause.text: Any person detained shall be brought before a judge and cannot be held without legal order.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether Wimalenthiran was detained in accordance with procedure established by law, including being brought before a Magistrate within the prescribed time and being held only under lawful detention orders.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that Wimalenthiran was detained at unauthorized places, was not produced before a Magistrate within the prescribed time, and that the detention orders were issued mechanically without proper satisfaction by the Secretary of Defence.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents argued that Wimalenthiran was detained under valid detention orders issued under Emergency Regulations and was produced before a Magistrate on 23 April 1994.
key_facts: Wimalenthiran was detained at Panagoda Army Camp, which was not an authorized place of detention at the relevant time.
He was not produced before a Magistrate within the time limits prescribed by Regulation 19(3).
Detention orders were issued by the Secretary of Defence without evidence that he was personally satisfied of the necessity of detention.
The Human Rights Task Force reported inability to get plausible explanation for detention and directed revocation of detention order.
Wimalenthiran was produced before a Magistrate only on 23 April 1994, after prolonged detention.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: Article 13(2) requires that any person detained must be brought before a judge according to procedure established by law and cannot be held without a lawful order. The Court emphasized that detention must be at authorized places and that the Secretary of Defence must be personally satisfied on material before issuing detention orders.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found that Wimalenthiran was detained at unauthorized places, including Panagoda Army Camp before it was gazetted as authorized. The Secretary did not demonstrate personal satisfaction on material to justify detention. Wimalenthiran was not produced before a Magistrate within the prescribed time, violating Article 13(2).
principles_established: Detention must be at places authorized by law and publicly notified.
Detention orders must be issued only after the detaining authority is personally satisfied on relevant material.
Detainees must be produced before a Magistrate within prescribed time limits.
Failure to comply with these procedures violates Article 13(2).
precedents_cited: Secretary of State v. Tameside 1976 3 ALL ER 665
Sasanasiritissa Thero v. De Silva and Others

outcome.holding: The Court declared that the detention of Wimalenthiran violated Article 13(2) because he was detained at unauthorized places, was not produced before a Magistrate within the prescribed time, and the detention orders were issued without proper satisfaction by the Secretary.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: The State was ordered to pay compensation and costs to Wimalenthiran.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 13(2) was central to the Court's decision as it governs the legality of detention, requiring production before a judge and lawful detention orders, all of which were violated in this case.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The Court found that Wimalenthiran was detained at unauthorized places, was not produced before a Magistrate within the prescribed time, and that the Secretary of Defence acted mechanically without personal satisfaction in issuing detention orders, violating Article 13(2).
